newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korea says Pyongyang apology may be imminent.
newsitem.headline: South Korea says Pyongyang apology may be imminent.

text.p: South Korea has details of an apology from Pyongyang over the intrusion of a North Korean submarine in September and the affair may be settled within a day, a foreign ministry official said on Saturday.
"We are aware of the details," the official in the ministry spokesman's office said by telephone.
"But I cannot confirm whether the government has received an official apology yet."
South Korean media have reported that an apology is imminent and U.S. and North Korean diplomats are thrashing out the final details in New York.
An apology from the North would ease military tensions on the Korean peninsula and could remove a threat to a key nuclear accord.
The Hankook Ilbo newspaper said in an early Sunday edition that North Korea had already handed over a letter of apology to the South expressing "deep regrets".
Asked to comment on the reports, the official said: "What you see in the newspapers comes pretty close.
"By tomorrow this whole affair should be wrapped up."

The Shark-class submarine landed 26 heavily armed North Koreans on an east coast beach in what South Korea said was a sabotage mission violating the terms of a truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
Twenty-four of the infiltrators were shot and killed, one was captured alive and one is still on the loose.
The agents killed several South Korean soldiers in shootouts and murdered civilians while dodging a massive dragnet in east coast mountains.

South Korea has demanded an apology as the price of resuming aid to the North and implementing a 1994 agreement between Washington and Pyongyang under which it will supply nuclear reactors to North Korea.
North Korea is on the verge of famine because of devastating floods and chronic economic mismanagement.
Domestic media reports said the apology was expected to be issued through North Korean state media.
The Hankook Ilbo said differences remained over the language to be used. North Korea was insisting on English only but South Korea wanted a Korean version as well.
The Joong-Ang Ilbo said the apology would pledge that incidents such as the submarine incursion would never occur again and the North would work for peace with the South.
Once an apology was received, South Korea would return the remains of the North Koreans, Yonhaps news agency reported.

The North Korean side in the New York talks is led by Li Hyong Chol, director of American affairs in Pyongyang's Foreign Ministry. Mark Minton, director of the State Department's office of Korean affairs, heads the U.S. side.

Resolving the submarine crisis would clear the way for progress on four-party talks proposed by the United States and South Korea with the North and China on a lasting peace to replace the Korean truce.
It would also allow further discussion on opening a U.S. diplomatic liaison office in Pyongyang, which has been bogged down over technical details.
Under the 1994 deal, North Korea abandoned its suspected nuclear weapons programme in exchange for safer nuclear reactors and shipments of fuel oil.
South Korea refuses to send technicians to the North to undertake crucial site inspection work for the reactors until it receives an apology.
